imperial.name: Rhubarb

actions.text:
Sow

Mar–Apr. Plant out seed-raised plants from Jul into autumn.

methods.text:
Plant crowns 

Choose a bought crown or divide a vigorous dormant plant. Set the piece upright with its buds just above the soil. Firm and water.

From seed 

Sow in pots under cover or in a nursery bed. Grow seedlings on before planting in their permanent positions. Allow an extra year before picking.

varieties.text:
Timperley Early

Early pink-and-green stems; also good for forcing to start the season.

Victoria

Established main-season crop of substantial green-red stalks for pies and preserves.

Raspberry Red

Tender, flavoursome red stalks. Buy named crowns/plants for consistency.

Glaskin's Perpetual

Traditional, economical seed-raised rhubarb; expect variation between plants.

Fulton's Strawberry Surprise

Vigorous plants with bright red stalks and a well-balanced flavour. A useful maincrop choice.

Stockbridge Arrow

Long, thick red stalks with good flavour. Also suitable for forcing.

text:
Rhubarb.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer

Rhubarb is a long-lived perennial vegetable, usually cooked as fruit. Large crowns give tart spring stems, green to red by variety; green stems are edible and colour does not show ripeness. Never eat the leaves. It suits cool climates and winter dormancy. Moist, drained, compost-rich soil, feeding, mulching, spring watering and flower removal keep crowns cropping for years. Yield varies with variety, age and conditions; leave enough foliage to rebuild the crown.

Quick facts
Harvest

Mar – Jun

Yield per mature plant

About 5 lb from a strong, established crown

Row spacing

36 in. between rows

Plant spacing

36 in. between plants

Plant crowns

While dormant, Nov–Mar.

Sow

Mar–Apr. Plant out seed-raised plants from Jul into autumn.

Ready in

Crowns: second spring, 12–18 months after planting; seed-grown plants a year longer

Recommended varieties
Timperley Early

Early pink-and-green stems; also good for forcing to start the season.

Victoria

Established main-season crop of substantial green-red stalks for pies and preserves.

Raspberry Red

Tender, flavoursome red stalks. Buy named crowns/plants for consistency.

Glaskin's Perpetual

Traditional, economical seed-raised rhubarb; expect variation between plants.

Fulton's Strawberry Surprise

Vigorous plants with bright red stalks and a well-balanced flavour. A useful maincrop choice.

Stockbridge Arrow

Long, thick red stalks with good flavour. Also suitable for forcing.

Key risks
Crown rot

Decay at the crown can cause weak, dull stems and rotting buds.

Slugs under forcing pots

Slugs may hide inside forcing pots or buckets and damage the tender forced stems.

Poor growth or stringy stems

Usually linked to dry soil, lack of organic matter, overcropping, or forcing the same crown too often.

Honey fungus

Honey fungus can cause rhubarb crowns to decline and die.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
80
STALKS & SHOOTS

Let young crowns build strength.

Leave the first year unpicked and take only a light crop in the second.

Eat the stalks, never the leaves.

Twist stalks away cleanly and leave plenty of foliage to feed the crown.

Soil & preparation
Choose a permanent, open position with rich, moist but well-drained soil. Avoid winter waterlogging and clear perennial weeds.
Prepare with compost, leaf mould or rotted manure. Allow space for vigorous roots at a plot edge.
Sowing & planting
Set the crown
Firm and water
Plant crowns 

Choose a bought crown or divide a vigorous dormant plant. Set the piece upright with its buds just above the soil. Firm and water.

From seed 

Sow in pots under cover or in a nursery bed. Grow seedlings on before planting in their permanent positions. Allow an extra year before picking.

Looking after the crop
Mulch annually with compost or well-rotted manure, keeping the central crown clear.
Water in dry spells. Dry spring soil gives short, stringy stalks.
Remove flower stalks promptly so energy goes into useful leaves and stems.
Force a strong crown in late winter under a light-proof pot. Check for slugs. After picking, uncover and rest it. Never force in consecutive years.
Harvesting & storage
Leave new crowns unpicked in year one. Pick lightly in year two. Always leave at least two-thirds of the stems and all thin ones.
Mature plants crop in spring and early summer; stop the usual harvest by late June so leaves rebuild the crown.
Grip near the base, twist and pull gently; avoid cut stumps. Remove and compost the poisonous leaf; eat only the stalk.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Crown rot	Bud and crown decay; stems become weak.	Remove badly affected crowns; improve drainage and use a clean site.
Slugs under forcing pots	Tender forced stems are chewed.	Check beneath forcing covers weekly and hand-remove slugs.
Poor growth or stringy stems	Thin, weak growth or stringy stems.	Water and mulch. Pick less and rest forced crowns.
Honey fungus	Declining crown. White fungal sheets in roots or crown.	Confirm diagnosis; remove infected roots and woody material.
Final tips

After forcing, take no more stalks that season and do not force the same crown the following year.

Healthy crown divisions retain a named variety; seedlings take longer and may vary.

Divide an ageing or crowded crown during dormancy and retain vigorous healthy pieces.

Leaves are not edible. Compost them and use only the stalks in the kitchen.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
81
STALKS & SHOOTS
